name: System design
routing_text: Designing large scale distributed systems: database sharding and partitioning, caching strategies and invalidation, replication, consistency and availability tradeoffs, transactions and isolation levels, distributed message queues, REST API design, latency, throughput and capacity estimation in a system design interview.
blurb: Distributed-systems decisions and the tradeoffs the speakers refuse to skip.

units.title: Modular monoliths need vertical slicing and encapsulation
units.summary: Creators argue that monoliths should be reorganized into independent, interchangeable modules aligned with business capabilities rather than traditional layered structures. Concrete tactics include vertical slices or package-by-feature, explicit public APIs, information hiding, and using compiler or module frameworks to enforce boundaries. They also stress that dependency management goes beyond code to shared databases and conventions, and that domain subdomains (core, generic, supporting) help estimate change frequency. Simon Brown sees package-by-feature versus layer as debatable, while Kevlin Henney warns that hidden dependencies like JSON or database conventions can silently couple modules.

units.title: Distributed systems make consistency a costly tradeoff
units.summary: These engineers agree that guaranteeing consistency across distributed databases is expensive and often conflicts with availability, latency, and operational simplicity. They cite replicas, read replicas, sharding, and two-phase commit as standard mechanisms, but point out that 2PC is slow and fragile and that cross-shard transactions should be avoided when possible. Several also stress that copied data isn't just duplication: a value like a price changes meaning as it flows from catalog to cart to order, so consistency choices must respect how data is used over time.

units.title: Latency fixes come at the cost of consistency
units.summary: Creators describe caching, CDNs, and sharding as core ways to cut latency in distributed systems, but they emphasize unavoidable tradeoffs: cached data can go stale, cross-shard queries stay expensive, and naive sharding causes massive data reshuffling until consistent hashing is introduced. They differ on the default approach: some treat external caching as the go-to solution, while others warn that regional isolation and cache expiry create single points of failure and hidden consistency problems. They also argue that evaluating system quality itself demands careful methods—using retrieval metrics like MRR and NDCG, and LLM judges that randomize order, allow ties, and use chain-of-thought reasoning to avoid bias.

units.title: Sharding splits data when vertical scaling fails
units.summary: Creators explain that database sharding—splitting data across multiple machines—becomes necessary when vertical scaling hits hardware limits and capacity thresholds like storage or write throughput are exceeded. They contrast sharding with partitioning, which splits data within a single server, and stress that sharding should not be reflexive; it should be justified with concrete numbers such as 70TB or 50,000 writes per second. They also note that sharding introduces trade-offs like routing, hot shards, and rebalancing, and recommend strategies such as consistent hashing to handle growth.

units.title: AI and subtle craft define today's software engineering
units.summary: These creators portray modern software engineering as a mix of AI-driven tools and deliberate human judgment. They repeatedly mention design tokens, icon weights, animation feel, and AI agents—from LangChain to custom-built agents—as ingredients for quality, whether shipping dozens of PRs per day or preparing interview projects from hackathons. A point of tension: some advocate building agents from scratch before using frameworks, while others warn against discarding older engineering skills—but all agree the field is moving toward a higher-level, more intentional practice.

rubrics.criterion: Draw module boundaries so that a single business change touches only one module.
rubrics.check: Pick a concrete feature change from the requirement list or history; trace every modified source and test file to a module. If the files land in more than one module, or a change forces re-testing of other modules, mark it failed.
rubrics.why: Without such localisation, most change effort goes into proving nothing else broke and the codebase becomes a tangled mess.
rubrics.unit_title: Modular monoliths need vertical slicing and encapsulation

evidence.title: Modularizing the Monolith - Jimmy Bogard - NDC Oslo 2024

rubrics.criterion: Make each module hide a design decision behind an interface that reveals as little as possible.
rubrics.check: For each module, write down the design decision it owns, then read the module's public entry points. If client code can reach a data structure, dependency or algorithm that is not part of that declared interface, fail.
rubrics.why: The interface is the contract clients depend on; exposing inner working makes every change a potential break to every other module.
rubrics.unit_title: Modular monoliths need vertical slicing and encapsulation

evidence.quote: every module is characterized by its knowledge of a design decision which it hides from all others

rubrics.criterion: Make every architectural component a first-class construct in code so diagrams and code mirror each other.
rubrics.check: For each box in the architecture diagram, locate a package, namespace, module or explicit type boundary in the code. If a box exists only as a 'conceptual grouping' of classes scattered across layers, fail; also fail if a top-level code grouping has no architectural box.
rubrics.why: If architectural abstractions are not first-class, architecture and code diverge and reasoning from diagrams is unreliable.
rubrics.unit_title: Modular monoliths need vertical slicing and encapsulation

rubrics.criterion: When a business event captures a value such as a price, persist that value as a snapshot in the historical record so later changes to the source value never mutate the record.
rubrics.check: Inspect an order/transaction record: is the price/amount stored at creation time and does it stay fixed even when the catalog price changes? If the record resolves the value from the current catalog at read time, fail.
rubrics.why: Users must not later see a better deal than the one they were charged; changing historical values makes the record meaningless.
rubrics.unit_title: Distributed systems make consistency a costly tradeoff

evidence.quote: I click place order and then that price shouldn't have changed there as well
evidence.model_quote: I click place order and then that price shouldn't have changed there as well

rubrics.criterion: Keep all data touched by one transaction on a single database/shard; do not use 2PC to make a cross-shard update atomic, and if a workflow must span shards, model it as a saga.
rubrics.check: For each atomic operation, list its reads and writes and verify they all land in one shard. Any design that uses a central coordinator or 2PC to commit across shards fails.
rubrics.why: When data lives on different shards the updates cannot happen in one atomic operation, and a failure between steps leaves an inconsistent state; 2PC is slow and fragile and can get stuck.
rubrics.unit_title: Distributed systems make consistency a costly tradeoff

rubrics.criterion: Replicated copies of data must be kept as exact matches of the primary, and all writes must go to the primary while reads are served from replicas.
rubrics.check: Find the write path for each replicated data item: if writes are accepted on any replica or replica contents can ever differ from the primary, fail. If replicas exist but reads are still served from the primary, fail the read-scaling design.
rubrics.why: If copies do not match, different users can see different values for the same data, so the system cannot be called consistent.
rubrics.unit_title: Distributed systems make consistency a costly tradeoff

rubrics.criterion: Place a cache in front of persistent storage for read-heavy data and set a TTL on cached entries.
rubrics.check: Trace the read path: a cache layer sits between the frontend and the database or cross-shard aggregation, and cached entries carry an expiration rather than living forever.
rubrics.why: The cache absorbs repeated reads and prevents every request from reaching the slower store, while the TTL prevents the cached result from going stale indefinitely.
rubrics.unit_title: Latency fixes come at the cost of consistency

rubrics.criterion: Use consistent hashing to distribute shards instead of a simple modulo function.
rubrics.check: Review the shard mapping: keys and shards are placed on a hash ring, optionally with virtual nodes; a plain key-modulo-N scheme fails the rule.
rubrics.why: With simple modulo, changing the shard count moves almost every key, forcing a massive redistribution of data that is an operational nightmare.
rubrics.unit_title: Latency fixes come at the cost of consistency

evidence.quote: consistent hashing places both the keys and the shards on this virtual ring
evidence.model_quote: consistent hashing places both the keys and the shards on this virtual ring
evidence.title: Sharding in System Design Interviews w/ Meta Staff Engineer

rubrics.criterion: Denormalize data so the related values used by a record live with that record instead of being resolved by joins at read time.
rubrics.check: Inspect the schema: records carry copied values such as price or related data colocated on the same shard, and reads do not require cross-shard scatter-gather or timestamp-based joins.
rubrics.why: Over-normalizing makes historical data meaning ambiguous, forces temporal joins, and leaves expensive cross-shard reads to be repeated, so related information must be stored together.
rubrics.unit_title: Latency fixes come at the cost of consistency

evidence.quote: you can denormalize your data so that related information lives together

rubrics.criterion: Choose a shard key that keeps every routine query on a single shard.
rubrics.check: List the main queries of the design, map each to the shard key, and mark how many shards each query must touch. If a routine query fans out to multiple shards, fail.
rubrics.why: Creators say constantly querying across all shards for a common use case signals the wrong shard key and that cross-shard queries should be the exception, not the norm.
rubrics.unit_title: Sharding splits data when vertical scaling fails

evidence.quote: cross shard queries should be the exception. They shouldn't be the norm
evidence.model_quote: Cross shard queries should be the exception. They shouldn't be the norm.

rubrics.criterion: Place shards with consistent hashing instead of a plain modulo of the shard count.
rubrics.check: Inspect the sharding scheme. Pass if keys and shards sit on a consistent-hash ring or use virtual nodes; fail if routing is plain key % number_of_shards with no stated rebalancing strategy.
rubrics.why: A modulo scheme requires nearly all data to move when the number of shards changes; consistent hashing eliminates that reshuffling problem.
rubrics.unit_title: Sharding splits data when vertical scaling fails

rubrics.criterion: Exhaust vertical scaling and read replicas before introducing sharding.
rubrics.check: Trace the capacity plan's order of escalation. Verify it first considers a larger single database and a read replica that offloads reads from the primary; fail if sharding is the proposed first response to growing traffic.
rubrics.why: The creators present vertical scaling as the obvious first instinct and read replicas as a way to keep the primary free for writes, with sharding's operational complexity only justified after those steps stop working.
rubrics.unit_title: Sharding splits data when vertical scaling fails

rubrics.criterion: Do not block a design or code review on style trivia; focus on whether it does what was asked.
rubrics.check: Read every review comment. Pass if each blocking comment names a functional gap, coupling, performance, security, or another real quality; fail if the only stated objection is casing, formatting, or an equally small detail.
rubrics.why: AI-generated code no longer makes syntax or expression mistakes, so the reviewable part is intent and outcome; nitpicking style hides the real engineering.
rubrics.unit_title: AI and subtle craft define today's software engineering

rubrics.criterion: Make quality attributes enforceable by adding automated fitness functions to the build process.
rubrics.check: Inspect the CI configuration and repository scripts. Pass if there is an automated check that asserts a structural quality metric such as cyclomatic complexity or coupling; fail if the pipeline only compiles, lints, or runs tests.
rubrics.why: Fitness functions prevent the codebase from silently degrading while teams sprint and take shortcuts.
rubrics.unit_title: AI and subtle craft define today's software engineering

evidence.quote: you can also use Fitness functions as a way to assert something about the fitness of your code base so cyclomatic complexity coupling
evidence.model_quote: you can also use Fitness functions as a way to assert something about the fitness of your code base so cyclomatic complexity coupling
evidence.title: Modular Monoliths • Simon Brown • GOTO 2018

rubrics.criterion: In design documentation, separate the transferable underlying principle from the specifics of the current stack.
rubrics.check: Read the rationale for each design decision. Pass if the document says which part is a principle you could carry elsewhere and which part is specific to this technology; fail if all reasoning is locked to one framework.
rubrics.why: People treat skills as mutually exclusive and discard prior knowledge when they change stacks, but principles from one context usually apply in the next.
rubrics.unit_title: AI and subtle craft define today's software engineering
